text: Teleportation sounds like science fiction, but the protocol is real, decades old, and worked out here with a fully verified numeric example. It's also the clearest demonstration that no-cloning and moving quantum information somewhere else are entirely compatible.

Alice holds a qubit in some state, 0.6 ket-zero plus 0.8 ket-one, that she wants to send Bob — crucially, without knowing what it actually is. If she already knew, she could just tell him the amplitudes directly. Alice and Bob each hold one qubit of a pre-shared Bell pair, Phi-plus. So there are three qubits total: Alice's unknown qubit, and each person's half of the entangled pair.

Alice performs a Bell-basis measurement on her two qubits together. Each of the four possible outcomes occurs with exactly probability 0.25, and depending on which one occurs, Bob's qubit ends up in a different raw state. For Phi-plus, Bob's qubit is already correct, 0.6, 0.8. For Phi-minus, it's 0.6, negative 0.8, and applying Z flips that sign back. For Psi-plus, it's 0.8, 0.6 — swapped — and applying X swaps it back. For Psi-minus, it's negative 0.8, 0.6, and applying X then Z recovers exactly 0.6, 0.8. Every one of the four cases ends up exactly matching the original state, no approximation.

Alice's outcome is effectively 2 classical bits, and she has to send those to Bob over an ordinary classical channel — a phone call, email, anything. Without that message, Bob has no way to know which correction to apply, and his qubit alone can't be used to extract the original state. Because Bob genuinely needs that classical message first, nothing has moved faster than that message could travel — at or below the speed of light, like any other signal.

Look closely at Alice's original qubit: her Bell measurement collapsed it. After the protocol, Alice no longer has the state in any form — only Bob does. Exactly one copy exists at every point in time, fully consistent with no-cloning: teleportation doesn't create a second copy while the first still exists, it moves the state, destroying the original as it recreates it elsewhere. The cost: one pre-shared entangled pair, one Bell measurement, and two classical bits per qubit teleported.
Next lesson runs the same resource trade in reverse: superdense coding, sending two classical bits using only one transmitted qubit.
